prompt:
You are helping me generate and evaluate brand-name candidates for my new company. First, ask me for: (1) a short description of what the company does, (2) my target industry/audience, (3) any words, tones, or themes I want included or avoided, and (4) which social platforms matter most to me (e.g., Instagram, X/Twitter, TikTok, LinkedIn).

Once I provide this, generate 15-20 distinct brand-name candidates that fit the business description and tone. For each candidate, do the following checks and record results in a table:

1. Domain availability: check whether the .com (and .io or .co if relevant) version of the name is registered, using a WHOIS lookup or domain registrar search.
2. Social handle availability: check whether the exact name (or close variant) is available as a username on the platforms I specified, by searching each platform directly.
3. Trademark conflict risk: search the USPTO Trademark Electronic Search System (TESS) or an equivalent public trademark database for exact or close matches in my industry class, and note any potential conflicts.

Score each candidate on a simple scale (e.g., green/yellow/red) for each of the three dimensions, then produce an overall ranking with your top 5 recommendations, briefly explaining the reasoning for each (memorability, relevance, risk level).

Done looks like: a clear table of all candidates with domain, social, and trademark status, plus a ranked shortlist of 5 names with rationale.

Report back with the full table, the top 5 shortlist, and any caveats (e.g., searches that were inconclusive or required manual verification). Do not register any domain, handle, or trademark — this is research only.

You are helping me evaluate brand-name candidates for my new company. Please ask me for: (1) the list of candidate names I want checked, (2) my preferred domain extensions (e.g., .com, .io, .co), (3) the social platforms I care about (e.g., Instagram, X/Twitter, TikTok, LinkedIn, YouTube), and (4) the country/jurisdiction whose trademark register matters most to me (e.g., USPTO for the US, EUIPO for the EU).

For each candidate name, do the following:
1. Domain availability: check the exact name plus close variants across my requested extensions using a WHOIS lookup or a domain registrar's availability search (e.g., via Namecheap or GoDaddy's public search page). Note which extensions are free vs. taken.
2. Social handle availability: visit each requested platform and check whether the exact handle (and one or two close variants) is available or already claimed. Note follower count/activity if the handle is taken, so I can gauge conflict severity.
3. Trademark conflicts: search the relevant trademark office's public database (e.g., USPTO TESS for the US, or the EUIPO database for the EU) for exact and close matches in relevant business categories. Also run a general web search for existing companies using the name to catch unregistered but active conflicts.

Compile a single table with columns: Name | Domain status (per extension) | Social handle status (per platform) | Trademark/usage conflict findings | Overall risk score (low/medium/high) with a one-line rationale.

Done looks like: every candidate has been checked across all three dimensions with sources noted, and the table is complete with an overall risk score for ranking. Report back the full table plus a short summary recommending the top 2-3 names with the fewest conflicts.

You are helping me pick a company name. Please act as the branding agent for the 'Present ranked candidates' step. If I haven't already given you the inputs, ask me for: (1) a short description of what my company does, (2) any keywords, themes, or style preferences for the name, (3) preferred domain TLDs (e.g. .com, .io), (4) which social platforms matter to me (e.g. X, Instagram, TikTop, LinkedIn), and (5) which country/jurisdiction(s) I care about for trademark risk.

Once you have that, generate 8-12 candidate brand names. For each candidate, check and record: domain availability for my preferred TLDs (use a domain lookup/WHOIS search), handle availability on the social platforms I named (search each platform directly), and potential trademark conflicts (search public trademark databases and general web/business registries for existing uses of the same or confusingly similar name in my industry).

Score each candidate on a simple scale (e.g. 1-5) for domain availability, handle availability, and trademark risk (lower risk = higher score), then compute a composite rank. Present the results as a single ranked table: Name | Domain status | Social handle status | Trademark risk notes | Composite score | Rank.

Below the table, write 2-3 sentences on the top 3 candidates explaining tradeoffs (e.g. strong domain but weak trademark clearance). Do not register any domain, handle, or trademark — just present the ranked findings and ask me which candidate(s) I'd like to move forward with. Report back the full table plus your top-3 recommendation summary.

You are helping me generate AI-created logo images for my brand. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) my brand name, (2) a short description of my brand's tone/industry (e.g., playful fintech, minimalist wellness), (3) any preferred colors, styles, or symbols, and (4) how many logo concepts I want (default to 4-6 if I don't specify).

Using OpenAI's image generation API (DALL-E) with my configured credentials, generate the requested number of distinct logo concepts based on the brand details I provide. Write clear prompts that specify: the brand name (if it should appear as text in the logo), a clean vector/flat-icon style suitable for a logo, transparent or white background, and the tone/colors I specified. Generate a few style variations (e.g., wordmark, icon-only, combination mark) if I haven't specified a single style.

Save each generated image locally or to my configured storage with a clear filename convention (e.g., brandname_logo_01.png, brandname_logo_02.png, etc.) so they can be reviewed and compared later.

Done looks like: a set of generated logo image files saved and accessible, covering the number of concepts and style variations requested, each reasonably matching the brand description I gave.

Report back to me with: the list of saved filenames/paths, a brief description of what each logo depicts (style, colors, layout), and any notes on prompts that produced weaker results so I can decide whether to regenerate before moving to the next step (storing and setting a primary logo).

You are helping me finish branding step brand_002:n2 — set the primary logo among the AI-generated logo images we already created and stored. Before acting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already clear: (1) the brand name/project this logo belongs to, (2) where the generated logo image files currently live (e.g., a specific folder path, cloud storage bucket, CMS media library, or database table), (3) how many candidate logos exist and any naming/versioning convention already in use, and (4) any selection criteria I want applied (e.g., preferred style, color, file format, or a specific filename I already like).

Once you have this, do the following: list the available logo candidates from the location I gave you, confirm which one I want as primary (if I haven't picked one, present the options with brief descriptions and ask me to choose — do not choose for me), then mark that file as the primary logo using whatever mechanism the storage system supports — this could mean renaming/copying it to a canonical filename (e.g., 'logo-primary.png'), setting a metadata flag or database field, or updating a manifest/config file that other tools reference. Make sure any other systems that reference 'the logo' (site header config, brand style guide doc, README) point to this same file if you have access to update them.

When done, report back: which logo file was set as primary, the exact location/identifier now marking it as primary, and any files or references you updated. If you could not determine where to write the 'primary' designation, tell me exactly what information you still need.

You are helping me generate color palette directions for my brand based on a set of brand adjectives (the descriptive words that define our brand personality, e.g., 'bold, trustworthy, modern' or 'warm, playful, approachable'). 

First, ask me for: (1) my brand adjectives (3-5 words), (2) my company/domain name, and (3) any existing brand constraints (e.g., a color we must include, an industry norm to avoid, accessibility requirements like WCAG contrast compliance).

Once I provide these, do the following:
1. Translate each adjective into color psychology associations (e.g., 'trustworthy' often maps to blues, 'playful' to bright/warm hues).
2. Propose 3 distinct palette directions, each with a clear name/theme (e.g., 'Confident Blue', 'Warm Optimism', 'Modern Minimal'). For each direction, specify: a primary color, one or two secondary/accent colors, and a neutral (background/text) color, each with hex codes.
3. For each palette, briefly explain how it reflects the given adjectives and note its likely emotional tone.
4. Flag any accessibility concerns (e.g., low contrast between text and background) for each palette.
5. Present the three directions in a clear side-by-side summary (table or bulleted comparison) so I can easily evaluate trade-offs.

Done looks like: three well-differentiated, named palette directions, each with hex codes for primary/secondary/neutral colors, a rationale tying back to my adjectives, and accessibility notes — ready for me to review and pick one (or request adjustments) in the next step.

Report back with the full comparison and your recommendation for which direction best fits the stated adjectives, along with reasoning. Do not finalize or lock in a palette — this is a proposal step only.

You are helping me choose a direction for our brand color palette. This is a subjective creative decision, so your job is to prepare well-researched options for me to review and decide on — not to make the final choice yourself.

First, ask me for any details you need if I haven't already given them: our company/domain name, a short description of what we do, our target audience, our industry, any competitor brands to differentiate from or align with, and any existing brand assets (logo, colors already in use) I should account for.

Then do the following:
1. Research color psychology and palette conventions relevant to our industry and audience.
2. Use a tool like Coolors (or similar palette generator) or your own design knowledge to generate 4-6 distinct palette directions (e.g., "bold and energetic," "minimal and trustworthy," "warm and organic," etc.), each with a short name and 1-2 sentence rationale tying it to our brand and audience.
3. For each direction, list the actual hex codes for a primary color, a secondary color, an accent color, and a neutral/background color.
4. Briefly note any competitor or industry conventions each direction aligns with or deliberately breaks from.
5. Compile all of this into a single clear document or message, organized so I can quickly compare directions side by side.

Done looks like: I have a concise, well-organized set of 4-6 palette direction options with hex codes, rationale, and industry context, ready for me to review.

Report back with the full list of palette directions and their details, then stop for human sign-off — do not select a final direction, apply any colors to brand assets, or make the choice on my behalf. Wait for me to tell you which direction I want to move forward with.

You are helping me finalize the brand color palette for my organization by checking WCAG contrast and accessibility compliance before it's locked in.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already provided:
- My domain or brand name
- The current candidate color palette (hex codes for primary, secondary, accent, background, and text colors)
- Any existing style guide, logo, or brand asset references
- Whether I have specific use cases to check (e.g., button text on brand background, links on white, dark-mode variants)

Once you have the palette, do the following:
1. Compute contrast ratios for all realistic foreground/background pairings likely to appear in the product or marketing site (e.g., body text on background, button label on button fill, link color on background, white text on dark brand color).
2. Evaluate each pairing against WCAG 2.1 standards: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+/14pt bold+) and UI components; note where AAA (7:1) is also met.
3. Flag every pairing that fails AA, and for each failing pair propose one or two adjusted hex values (slightly darker/lighter shades of the same brand color) that would pass while staying visually close to the original intent.
4. Check the palette for color-blind safety (e.g., avoid relying on red/green alone to convey meaning) and note any concerns.
5. Produce a clear table: color pair, hex codes, contrast ratio, pass/fail for AA and AAA, and recommended fix if failing.

Done looks like: a complete contrast audit table covering all key pairings, with pass/fail status and concrete hex-code remediation suggestions for any failures, plus a short summary of overall accessibility risk.

Report back with the full table, the summary, and a final list of the recommended (possibly adjusted) palette hex codes ready for my review. Do not change official brand assets or publish anything — just prepare this analysis, since finalizing the palette remains a human step.

You are helping me set our finalized brand color palette as design tokens (variables) inside {{vendor}}, our design tool. 

Before starting, ask me for: (1) the final list of brand colors with names and hex values (e.g. Primary, Secondary, Accent, Neutral shades, Success/Error/Warning if defined), (2) the {{vendor}} workspace/team or project where these tokens should live, and (3) whether we need multiple modes/themes (e.g. Light and Dark) or just one default mode.

Once you have this, using your configured credentials and {{vendor}}'s API or plugin/token-management interface:
1. Create or open the relevant design file/library in {{vendor}}.
2. Create a color variable/token collection for our brand palette if one doesn't already exist.
3. Add each brand color as a named token with the correct hex value, matching the names I gave you.
4. If multiple modes were requested, set up those modes and assign correct values per mode.
5. Verify the tokens are saved and visible in the tool's variables/tokens panel, and that names and values exactly match what I provided.
6. If the API/plugin surface requires publishing or enabling library sharing for the tokens to be usable across files, complete that action as it is a routine configuration step, not a sign-off decision.

When done, report back: the name of the token collection/library, the full list of tokens created with their names, hex values, and mode assignments (if any), and a link or path to where they live in {{vendor}}. If any color name was ambiguous or you had to make a judgment call on naming/structure, flag it clearly in your report so I can review. Do not invent colors or modes I have not provided — ask me if anything is missing.

You are helping me begin our SOC 2 Type I compliance journey by preparing the account creation process for {{vendor}}, a compliance-automation platform. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for any missing inputs you need: our company legal name, primary business domain, the email address that should be the account owner (likely a founder or compliance officer), and any preferred workspace/organization name.
2. Navigate to {{vendor}}'s signup/registration page and fill out the account creation form using the details I provide, using your configured credentials for any single sign-on or email verification steps if applicable.
3. Progress through the signup flow as far as possible without finalizing — this includes selecting a plan/tier if prompted (flag any pricing or contract terms you encounter for my review), entering company details, and reaching the point where terms of service or a vendor agreement must be accepted.
4. Do NOT accept any terms of service, click any final "agree," "submit," "confirm purchase," or "create account" button that binds us to a contract. Do not approve account ownership on our behalf.
5. Prepare a summary for me including: the exact form fields you filled in, any plan/pricing options presented, the terms of service or vendor agreement text (or a link to it) that will need to be accepted, and screenshots or a description of the final confirmation screen you stopped at.
6. Stop for human sign-off before any terms are accepted or the account is finalized — this step requires an officer to explicitly approve the vendor contract and account ownership.

Report back with: the inputs you used, the current state of the signup form, any outstanding decisions (plan selection, billing details), and a clear note that you have paused at the terms-of-service/final-confirmation step awaiting my explicit approval.

You are helping me complete the 'Connect integrations' step of our SOC 2 Type I setup in {{vendor}}, our compliance automation platform. Please prepare (but do not finalize) the integration connections needed for evidence collection.

First, ask me for: (1) my {{vendor}} account login/workspace details, (2) the list of systems we need connected — typically our cloud provider(s), identity provider, code hosting, HR system, MDM, and ticketing tool, and (3) whether we have any custom/on-prem systems not in the standard catalog.

Then, using my configured credentials, log into {{vendor}} and navigate to its integrations catalog. For each standard system I name, locate the correct integration entry, confirm it uses read-only scopes where offered, and prepare it for connection — filling in any required configuration fields, but stop before triggering the OAuth authorization or credential-grant flow, since that requires my explicit consent per system.

For any custom or on-prem systems not in the catalog, check whether {{vendor}} supports custom connections via a documented API; if so, describe in words how a developer would create and list such connections so evidence can be pushed manually. Draft the specific setup steps for a developer to implement this, but do not execute API calls that grant access.

Produce a checklist listing: each system to connect, the scopes/permissions each integration will request, and which step requires my manual OAuth approval in the {{vendor}} UI. Flag any integration whose required permissions look broader than read-only so I can review them.

When your checklist and draft configurations are ready, present them to me and stop for human sign-off before any authorization is granted or integration is finalized.

You are helping me generate the initial set of security policies for our SOC 2 Type I journey using {{vendor}}, our compliance automation platform. If you don't already know them, ask me for: (1) our {{vendor}} account login/workspace details (confirm you can use your configured credentials to access it), (2) our company legal name and domain, and (3) the list of employees/roles who will need to accept policies.

Actions to take:
1. Log into {{vendor}} using your configured credentials.
2. Locate the policy template library and fetch the standard SOC 2 policy set (e.g., Information Security, Access Control, Data Classification, Incident Response, Change Management, Vendor Management, Business Continuity).
3. If {{vendor}} offers a built-in AI assistant, delegate drafting/customization of each policy to it, tailoring placeholders (company name, scope, roles, review cadence) to our details.
4. Set up or confirm version control and an approval workflow within {{vendor}} so each policy has a draft state, an editor history, and a designated approver.
5. Configure per-employee acceptance tracking so the platform will notify staff and log acknowledgments once policies are published.
6. Compile a summary checklist listing every policy generated, its current draft status, assigned approver, and any open placeholders needing my input.

Do not publish, finalize, or mark any policy as approved, and do not trigger employee acceptance notifications. This step requires that a human explicitly approve before changes are applied, so you must stop for human sign-off once drafts and the checklist are ready.

Report back with: the list of policies drafted, a link or path to each in {{vendor}}, the approval workflow status, any unresolved placeholders, and a clear note that you are stopping for human sign-off before publishing.

You are helping me prepare the SOC 2 Type I policy set inside Vanta ahead of human compliance review. Do not finalize, publish, or mark any policy as approved—your job is to draft and organize, not to approve.

Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available: my company domain, Vanta account access confirmation (assume I use my configured credentials), a description of our actual security practices (e.g., access control model, data handling, incident response process, vendor management, infrastructure/cloud setup), and any existing internal policy documents or wiki pages I want reflected.

Actions to take:
1. Log into Vanta and pull up the default policy templates it generated for our SOC 2 Type I program (e.g., Information Security Policy, Access Control Policy, Data Classification Policy, Incident Response Policy, Vendor Management Policy, etc.).
2. For each policy, compare the template language against the operational details I gave you and draft edits so the wording matches what we actually do (systems used, roles/titles, approval chains, review cadence).
3. Flag any policy sections where the template assumes a control we don't have in place, or where our practice is stricter/looser than the template implies—list these clearly as open questions rather than guessing.
4. Organize your output as a per-policy diff or summary: what Vanta's default said, what you propose changing, and why.

Done looks like: every relevant policy has a drafted redline and a list of unresolved judgment calls, all staged in Vanta as unpublished edits (not applied/approved).

Report back with the full list of policies reviewed, the proposed changes for each, and the open questions needing compliance/legal judgment. Then stop for human sign-off before any policy is approved or applied in Vanta.

You are helping me configure automated compliance tests in {{vendor}}, our compliance-automation platform, as part of starting our SOC 2 Type I journey. Before starting, ask me for: (1) my {{vendor}} account/workspace details or confirm I'm already logged in with configured credentials, (2) which systems/integrations are already connected (cloud provider, identity provider, version control, etc.), and (3) any custom frameworks or controls beyond the standard SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria I want included.

Once you have this, use {{vendor}}'s dashboard or API to review the library of available automated tests, and pull the current list of tests already enabled versus available but inactive (use the platform's test-listing API or dashboard view to retrieve this). Map each relevant Trust Services control to an available automated test, noting which tests can run against our connected systems today versus which require an additional integration first. If I've indicated custom controls, draft proposed custom test definitions and their evidence requirements alongside the built-in ones.

Produce a clear configuration plan: a table listing each control, the proposed test, its evidence-collection schedule, and whether it's net-new or already active. Do NOT enable, activate, or apply any test configuration changes yourself — a human must explicitly approve before changes are applied. Present the full plan and stop for human sign-off.

Report back with: the full proposed test/control mapping, any gaps where no automated test exists yet (flag for manual evidence), and any integrations needed before certain tests can run, so I can review and approve before you or I apply anything in {{vendor}}.

You are helping me remediate failing compliance test results in our Vanta SOC 2 Type I monitoring dashboard. Please do the following:

1. If you don't already have it, ask me for access details or confirm you can use my configured credentials to log into Vanta.
2. Pull the current list of failing tests from the Vanta dashboard, grouped by integrated service (e.g., AWS, Google Workspace, GitHub, identity provider, HR system) and by control category (access control, encryption, logging, vulnerability management, etc.).
3. For each failing test, identify the root cause (e.g., MFA not enforced, unencrypted storage bucket, missing log retention policy, inactive user account not deprovisioned, missing vendor security review).
4. Draft a specific remediation plan per failing test: what setting needs to change, in which system, and the exact steps to change it. Where a fix requires a policy document update, draft the revised policy language.
5. Prioritize the list by risk severity and ease of fix, and flag any tests that require a business decision (e.g., choosing a new access policy) rather than a pure technical fix.
6. Compile everything into a single remediation report: test name, current status, root cause, proposed fix, system/owner affected, and estimated effort.

Do not make any configuration changes, update any policies, close out any tests, or mark anything remediated in Vanta yourself. Every change must be explicitly approved by a human before it is applied, since a human must explicitly approve before changes are applied. Prepare the full remediation plan and pre-filled drafts, then stop for human sign-off.

Report back with the complete failing-tests list, your remediation plan for each item, and a clear summary of which items are ready for one-click approval versus which need a policy decision from me first.

You are helping me operationalize the 'Employee security training' step of our SOC 2 Type I journey in Vanta. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for our Vanta account domain/login context if not already known, our employee roster (or the HR/people-ops source of truth, e.g. Google Workspace, BambooHR, or a spreadsheet I provide), and the deadline I want to set for training completion.
2. Using your configured credentials, log into Vanta and confirm the security training module is enabled and assigned to all current employees and contractors who need it (per our policy scope).
3. Cross-check the Vanta employee list against my roster to flag any missing, duplicate, or offboarded accounts, and prepare a list of discrepancies for me to resolve.
4. Draft a short reminder email/Slack message I can send to employees who haven't completed training yet, including the deadline and a link to the Vanta training portal.
5. Set up a recurring check (daily or every few days, your recommendation) where you poll Vanta's training completion dashboard and report back the current completion percentage, names of employees still pending, and any overdue past the deadline.
6. Note explicitly that actually completing each individual's training modules remains a human step — this is third-party-wait: each employee must log in and finish their own modules on their own schedule, and no agent action can complete that for them.

Done looks like: training assigned to all employees in Vanta, discrepancies list prepared, reminder draft ready, and a monitoring cadence established so I get regular completion-status updates until 100% is reached.

Report back with: current completion %, list of outstanding employees, any roster mismatches found, and the reminder draft text for my review.

You are helping me prepare to engage a SOC 2 Type I auditor as part of our Vanta compliance journey. This is a policy-gate step: you must prepare everything needed but cannot select a firm, negotiate terms, or sign any engagement letter — that requires an authorized officer's decision.

First, ask me for: (1) our company legal name and domain, (2) our target SOC 2 Type I audit window/deadline if known, (3) whether we have Vanta's list of pre-approved/integrated audit firm partners available, or whether I want you to compile a shortlist of reputable SOC 2 audit firms from public information, and (4) any budget range or firm-size preference (boutique vs. established).

Then do the following:
1. Research and compile a comparison list of 3-5 candidate SOC 2 audit firms (or use Vanta's partner directory if I provide access), including for each: firm name, relevant experience with SOC 2 Type I, typical turnaround time, and general pricing range if publicly available.
2. Draft an outreach email template requesting a proposal/engagement letter from shortlisted firms, referencing our company, desired report type (Type I), and target timeline.
3. Prepare a checklist of information the chosen auditor will likely need from us (system description scope, control list, policy documents, evidence collection status in Vanta).
4. Summarize the shortlist, draft outreach email, and checklist in a single document.

Done looks like: a ready-to-send comparison summary, outreach draft, and information checklist, all pending my review. Do not contact any firm, negotiate pricing, or sign or submit any engagement letter on my behalf — stop for human sign-off once materials are prepared. Report back with the shortlist, drafts, and a clear note that firm selection and contract signature remain my decision to make.

You are helping me monitor and prepare for the completion of our SOC 2 Type I audit, which we are running through Vanta with an independent third-party auditing firm. The actual conduct and sign-off of the audit examination remains a human step performed by the third-party auditor and cannot be completed or accelerated by you.

First, ask me for anything you need that you don't already have: our company domain, our Vanta account login status (confirm I can access it with my configured credentials), the name of the auditing firm we've engaged (if selected), and the expected audit start/end dates if known.

Then, using my configured credentials, log into our Vanta dashboard and:
1. Check the current audit status (e.g., evidence collection, auditor review, report drafting).
2. Compile a summary of any outstanding evidence requests, failed/at-risk controls, or unresolved policy gaps flagged in Vanta that could delay or block the auditor.
3. Identify any open auditor questions or requests visible in Vanta or via any auditor communication tools we use, and draft clear, factual responses I can review (do not send them yourself).
4. Note the last-updated timestamp on the audit status so we can track progress over time.

Do not sign, approve, submit, or communicate directly with the auditor on my behalf — only prepare drafts and summaries for my review.

Report back with: (a) current audit status and stage, (b) any outstanding items requiring my input or action, (c) drafted responses to auditor requests if any exist, and (d) a recommended date/time for you to poll Vanta again for status updates, since final completion depends on the auditor's independent testing timeline and remains a human step.

You are helping me prepare for the SOC 2 Type II observation window and scope negotiation with our audit firm. This negotiation itself remains a human step, since it requires back-and-forth professional judgment between me and the auditor's team based on their methodology and our risk profile — you cannot drive it.

What I need you to do instead is prepare all the materials so the actual conversation goes smoothly:

1. Ask me for: our company domain, the trust services criteria we're pursuing (e.g., Security, Availability, Confidentiality), the date our Type I report was issued, our current infrastructure/vendor stack, and the name of our audit firm if known.
2. Draft a one-page briefing document summarizing: our Type I scope and any exceptions noted, our proposed observation window (research typical ranges of 3, 6, or 12 months and note tradeoffs for enterprise buyer expectations), and any system/control changes since Type I that could affect scope.
3. Draft a list of clarifying questions to bring to the auditor, such as: what evidence cadence they expect, whether any new systems or subservice organizations should be added to scope, and how they handle control changes mid-window.
4. Prepare a checklist of internal readiness items (evidence collection tooling in place, control owners identified, calendar blocked for the window) so I can confirm we're ready to commit to a start date.

Once these materials are drafted, stop for human sign-off — do not contact the auditor, propose dates on my behalf, or finalize scope. Report back with the briefing document, the question list, and the readiness checklist, clearly labeled, and flag any gaps where you need more information from me before finishing the draft.

You are helping me configure continuous control monitoring in {{vendor}} for our SOC 2 Type II observation window. Before starting, ask me for: (1) our {{vendor}} account access confirmation (use your configured credentials), (2) the list of systems in our stack that need connecting (cloud providers, identity provider, HR system, code hosting, MDM, ticketing tool), and (3) my preferred alert destination (Slack channel, email address, or ticketing queue) for control failures.

Once you have this, please:
1. Log into {{vendor}} and review the integrations catalog; connect each system I listed using read-only scopes where offered, confirming successful connection for each.
2. Use the {{vendor}} API to call GET /controls and pull the full list of controls now being monitored — flag any Trust Services controls that appear unmonitored or lack a connected data source.
3. Use the {{vendor}} API to call GET /monitoring-tests to confirm automated tests are actively scheduled against our connected systems, and note the test frequency for each.
4. Configure or verify alert routing so that control failures and configuration drift notify us at the destination I specified, with enough context (control name, system, failure detail) to act on.
5. Compile a summary showing: systems connected, controls actively monitored vs. any gaps, monitoring test coverage, and alert routing status.

Done looks like: every system in our stack is connected with read-only access, all applicable SOC 2 controls show active automated monitoring tests, and alerts are routed to our chosen channel with actionable detail — no manual screenshot or CSV evidence collection remains.

Report back with the connected systems list, any controls or systems still needing attention, the monitoring test coverage summary, and confirmation of alert routing, so I can address gaps before the observation window evidence is relied upon.

You are helping me track the SOC 2 Type II observation window, the 3–12 month period during which my controls must operate continuously before our auditor can begin fieldwork. The actual passage of time and the auditor's eventual attestation remains a human step you cannot accelerate or perform — please do not attempt to simulate or skip it.

What I need from you now is preparation and monitoring support. First, ask me for: (1) the start date of the observation window, (2) the planned end date (based on the window length I chose, e.g., 3, 6, or 12 months), (3) which compliance automation platform I use (if any) for continuous evidence collection, and (4) the auditor firm's name and contact if already engaged.

Once I provide these, please:
1. Create a simple tracking record (a checklist or timeline doc) showing the start date, end date, and key milestones (e.g., monthly control-evidence check-ins, mid-window review, pre-fieldwork prep deadline).
2. Draft a recurring reminder schedule (weekly or monthly) for me to verify that evidence collection is running without gaps — flag if my compliance platform shows any control test failures or missing evidence during this period.
3. Prepare a pre-fieldwork readiness checklist covering: management assertion draft, evidence completeness review, and auditor coordination steps, so I can act quickly once the window closes.

You are helping me remediate the critical and high severity findings from our annual penetration test so we can request a retest and satisfy our SOC 2 auditor. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the pen test findings report or export, (2) access to our issue tracker (e.g., Jira, Linear, GitHub Issues) using my configured credentials, and (3) the repos/systems/environments affected by each finding.

Actions to take:

2. For each finding, check the issue tracker for an existing ticket; if none exists, create one with the finding details, severity label, and a due date reflecting urgency (criticals fastest).

5. Update each ticket's status as work progresses (open, in-progress, fixed-pending-verification).
6. Compile a remediation summary listing each critical/high finding, its ticket link, current status, and evidence of the fix (commit link, config diff, or description) for eventual submission to the pen test firm for retest.

Done looks like: every critical and high finding has a tracked ticket, a proposed or completed fix, and a status; low-risk fixes are drafted as ready-to-review PRs but not merged or deployed — that remains a human step. Report back with the full list of findings, their ticket links, fix status, and which items still need a human decision or deployment approval.

Do not decide the priority tier or resourcing yourself — that judgment call belongs to me as the deal/security owner.

When the brief is ready, present it to me clearly and stop for human sign-off so I can decide how to prioritize this questionnaire against other deals and assign resourcing.

5. Add a short citation note per answer (which policy doc or prior questionnaire it was pulled from) so reviewers can verify quickly.

When done, produce an updated spreadsheet or document with: drafted answers, source citations, and a status column (Drafted / Needs Source / Needs Review). Give me a summary count of how many rows fall into each status category, plus a list of the flagged high-risk rows with a one-line reason for each. You are helping me prepare the security-review package for the risky answers in our security questionnaire draft, ahead of sign-off by our security lead. Produce a summary table with: month, gross burn, net burn, cash balance, and runway in months — plus a short narrative paragraph suitable for inclusion in a board deck.

3. Separately, ask me to confirm any states where the company leases, owns, or operates a physical office, warehouse, or other facility, even if no employees are based there.
4. Combine both sources into a single deduplicated list of states, noting for each state whether the trigger is 'employee(s)' or 'office/facility' or both, and roughly how many employees are in each state.
5. Flag any ambiguous cases (e.g., remote employees who relocated recently, employees in multiple states, or contractors vs. employees) for my review.

Done looks like a clear table or list of states with employee counts and office presence, plus any flagged ambiguities. Report back the final state list, the source(s) used to compile it, and any open questions I need to resolve before the next step (filing foreign qualifications).

You are helping me determine whether my company needs to register as a foreign entity (obtain a 'foreign qualification') in any U.S. states beyond our state of incorporation/formation. Before starting, ask me for: (1) my company's state of incorporation/formation and entity type (LLC, C-corp, etc.), (2) a list of all states where we currently have employees (remote or in-office), physical offices, warehouses, or other physical presence, and (3) our company's legal name and EIN if available for reference.

Once I provide this, for each state listed where we do NOT already hold a foreign qualification, research that state's Secretary of State (or equivalent business registration agency) website to determine: whether our activities (having employees, an office, or other presence) trigger a 'doing business' threshold requiring foreign qualification, what the specific filing is called, the filing fee, required documents (e.g., certificate of good standing from home state), and whether a registered agent is required in that state.

Compile your findings into a table with columns: State | Foreign Qualification Required? (Yes/No/Unclear) | Basis for Trigger | Filing Name | Fee | Registered Agent Required? | Source URL. Flag any states where the answer is ambiguous based on official guidance, and note if professional legal advice is recommended for a final determination.

Do not file anything or submit any registration — this step is only to identify which states require action. Report back with the completed table, a short summary of which states clearly need foreign qualification, and any open questions.

You are helping me prepare (but not submit) foreign qualification filings for our company in the states where we have employees or offices. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: (a) our company's legal name, entity type, and home state of incorporation; (b) a list of states where we currently have employees, offices, or other physical presence; (c) our registered agent details or whether we need to identify a registered agent in each new state; (d) our EIN and formation date; (e) our current Certificate of Good Standing status (or note if we need to request one from our home state).

2. For each state on the list, research that state's Secretary of State (or equivalent) portal requirements for filing a 'foreign qualification' or 'application for authority to transact business.' Note the required form name, filing fee, whether a Certificate of Good Standing is required, and typical processing time.

3. Pre-fill each state's application draft with our company details as far as possible, and compile a checklist per state showing: form name, fee, required attachments, registered agent requirement, and where an officer's signature/attestation about nexus is required.

4. Flag clearly that determining 'nexus' (whether presence in a state legally triggers a filing requirement) and attesting to it is a legal judgment call that only a company officer can make, and that no filing should be submitted until an officer has reviewed and approved each state's determination and draft.

5. Compile everything into a single summary document per state, organized for easy officer review.

Do not submit, sign, or attest to any filing on my behalf — this requires an officer's legal attestation and must stop for human sign-off. Once the drafts and checklists are ready, report back with the full list of states, filing costs, required documents, and a note confirming the package is ready for officer review and sign-off.

You are helping me prepare for filing my company's state annual report by first gathering all the incorporation and filing details we'll need. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for any of these details you don't already have access to: my company's legal name, state of incorporation, entity type (LLC, C-Corp, etc.), incorporation/formation date, registered agent name and address, principal business address, EIN, and the state's business entity ID or file number.

2. If I have credentials configured for our corporate records system, document management tool, or the Secretary of State's online business portal, use those configured credentials to look up and confirm: our current registered agent of record, our current officers/directors or members/managers on file, our business entity status (active/good standing), and the last date an annual report was filed.

3. Check whether there's a specific due date or filing window for our annual report based on our state of incorporation and formation anniversary, and note it clearly.

4. Compile everything into a single organized summary document (a checklist or table) listing: all gathered details, any discrepancies you noticed between our internal records and the state's records, and any information that is still missing or needs my confirmation before filing.

Done looks like: a complete, organized draft summary of all incorporation and filing details needed for the annual report, with any gaps or mismatches clearly flagged for me to resolve.

Report back with: the compiled summary, a list of any missing or uncertain items you need me to supply or confirm, and the filing deadline you identified. Do not submit or file anything yet — this step is only about gathering and organizing the information.

You are helping me file my company's state annual report through my state of incorporation's Secretary of State (or equivalent agency) online filing portal, to keep the company in good standing.

Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have:

- Company legal name and state entity/file number
- The portal URL if I have it, or confirm I want you to locate the correct state filing site
- Current registered agent name and address

- Officer/director or member/manager names and addresses (as required by that state's form)
- Any changes to report since the last filing

Actions to take:

2. Log in using my configured credentials, or locate the entity via the file number if no login is required.
3. Enter or verify all required fields on the deterministic annual report form: entity name, registered agent, addresses, officers/managers, and any other state-required data.
4. Calculate or confirm the filing fee due.
5. Complete the form through the payment/review step, filling in all required data accurately.
6. Stop before final submission and payment authorization.

Done looks like: the annual report form is fully filled out and validated on the portal, with all data double-checked against what I provided, and the filing is staged and ready to submit, but not yet submitted or paid.

Report back with: the state and portal used, a summary of all data entered, the calculated fee, and confirmation that everything is staged and ready. Then stop for human sign-off, since final submission and payment must be authorized by me.

You are helping me close out our state annual report filing by properly saving the confirmation receipt. Context: I already filed (or am about to file) our company's annual report with our state of incorporation's Secretary of State (or equivalent business filing agency) office, typically through their online business filing portal.

Please do the following:
1. Ask me for: (a) which state we're incorporated in, (b) the confirmation number or receipt reference from the filing (if I have it), and (c) where I'd like records stored (e.g., a specific cloud drive folder, document management system, or local directory) using my configured credentials.
2. If the filing was completed online, retrieve or help me download the confirmation receipt/PDF from the state's filing portal using my configured credentials — this may include the payment receipt, the filed annual report copy, and any confirmation email.
3. Rename the file clearly, following a consistent convention such as: [CompanyName]_[State]_AnnualReport_[FilingYear]_Confirmation.pdf
4. Save the file to the designated storage location, organized in a folder structure like /Corporate Records/Annual Reports/[State]/[Year]/.
5. Log the filing details in a simple tracking record (spreadsheet or doc) noting: state, filing date, confirmation number, amount paid, and next year's due date.
6. Verify the file saved correctly and is accessible/readable.

Done looks like: the confirmation receipt is saved in the correct location with a clear filename, the tracking log is updated, and I have a copy of the confirmation number readily accessible for future reference or state inquiries.

Report back with: the file location/path where the receipt was saved, the confirmation number captured, and the next annual report due date so I can calendar it. If you cannot access the filing portal or locate the receipt, tell me exactly what's missing so I can provide it.

You are helping me track startup runway. For this step, fetch current cash account balances from {{vendor}}, our startup banking platform, using its documented public API and my already-configured credentials.

Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have: (1) the {{vendor}} name/instance if not set, (2) confirmation that API access is configured, and (3) which accounts (by name or ID) should be included, or confirm 'all accounts' as default.

Actions to take:
1. Call {{vendor}}'s account-balances API endpoint to pull the current balance for every active cash account tied to our business.
2. If {{vendor}} exposes a balance-history endpoint, also pull recent daily balance history for each account so we can see trend, not just a snapshot.
3. If {{vendor}} supports webhooks for balance/transaction events, check whether a subscription already exists; if not, note that as a setup gap but do not attempt to configure alerts, top-ups, or transfers — that's outside this step's scope.
4. Normalize the results into a simple table: account name, account ID, currency, current balance, as-of timestamp, and (if available) balance 7/30 days ago.

Done looks like: you have pulled balances for all in-scope accounts, captured a timestamp for freshness, and flagged any accounts that returned errors or stale data.

Report back with: the balance table described above, total cash across accounts, any accounts that failed to sync (with the error), and whether balance-history and webhook data were available. Do not attempt to move money, set alerts, or change account settings — only fetch and report balances.

You are helping me analyze monthly spend as part of tracking company runway. I use {{vendor}} as my expense-management platform. Please use my configured credentials to connect to {{vendor}} and pull all outgoing transactions for the most recently completed calendar month.

If you don't already know my {{vendor}} account details or which entity/workspace to query, ask me first.

Actions to take:
1. Retrieve the full list of transactions for the month using {{vendor}}'s transaction listing or spend-analysis capability (API, CLI, or MCP tool as available).
2. Break down total spend by category, merchant, and team/department where that data is available.
3. Identify the largest individual expenses (top 10 by amount) and flag any duplicates, unusual spikes, or transactions missing a category/memo/receipt.
4. Calculate total monthly burn (sum of outgoing transactions) and compare it to the prior month's burn if that data is accessible, noting the percentage change.
5. Summarize any AI-generated insights or anomaly flags {{vendor}} surfaces natively (e.g., suspected duplicates, fraud flags, miscategorized spend).

Done looks like: a clear monthly spend report showing total burn, top spend categories, top merchants, top individual transactions, month-over-month change, and a short list of flagged anomalies or uncategorized items needing review.

Report back to me with: the total monthly burn figure, a breakdown table (category/merchant/amount), the month-over-month trend, and a bullet list of anomalies or items needing manual review. Do not take any corrective action on flagged transactions (e.g., recategorizing, disputing, or approving) — just surface them for my review.

You are helping me calculate our current cash runway using {{vendor}}, our accounting system. Please do the following:

1. If you don't already have it, ask me for: (a) confirmation that your access to {{vendor}} is via my configured credentials, and (b) which bank/cash accounts should count as 'cash on hand' (in case we have accounts to exclude, like restricted deposits).

2. Using {{vendor}}'s reporting or API access, pull the current total cash balance across all included accounts.

3. Generate a cash-flow statement (or P&L plus balance sheet if cash-flow isn't directly available) for the trailing 3 full months. Use this to compute average monthly net burn (cash out minus cash in, excluding one-time or non-operating items if you can identify them — flag anything you exclude and why).

4. Calculate runway in months: current cash balance ÷ average monthly burn. Also calculate a projected zero-cash date by adding that many months to today's date.

5. Cross-check the burn number against the general ledger or trial balance for the same period to confirm consistency, noting any material discrepancy.

6. If {{vendor}} supports filtering/grouping by class, location, or tag, pull a secondary breakdown of burn by department or category so I can see what's driving spend.

When done, report back with: current cash balance, average monthly burn (with the trailing-period dates used), runway in months, projected zero-cash date, any exclusions or assumptions you made, and the department/category burn breakdown if available. Flag any data gaps (e.g., missing months, unreconciled accounts) that could affect accuracy rather than guessing at numbers.

You are helping me choose a cap table management tool ({{vendor}}) for my startup so I can track all investments — including informal rounds — on a live, single source of truth from day one.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already clear: my company domain/name, my jurisdiction (e.g., Delaware C-corp, UK Ltd, etc.), whether I currently track equity in a spreadsheet or another tool, roughly how many stakeholders/share classes/SAFEs/option grants exist today, and my budget expectations.

3. Whether it can serve as a live single source of truth for share classes, certificates, SAFEs, and option grants that investors and auditors can rely on.

For each candidate, summarize pricing tiers, ease of migration, export policy, integrations, and any limitations relevant to an early-stage startup with informal/pre-priced rounds. Present a comparison table of at least 3 realistic options with pros/cons for my specific situation.

Do not sign up for any service, enter payment details, or make the final selection yourself — this is a business decision that depends on my priorities and future fundraising plans, so it remains a human step. Prepare the comparison, a recommendation with reasoning, and a checklist of next steps (account creation, data migration prep, inviting stakeholders) so I can act quickly once I decide.

Report back with: the comparison table, your top recommendation and why, and the prepared checklist, then stop for human sign-off before proceeding further.

You are helping me enter founding shares into our cap table software (e.g., Carta, Pulley, or a spreadsheet-based tracker — use whichever platform I already have set up). Please ask me for any of the following if not already provided:

Save each entry and confirm it appears correctly in the cap table summary view (correct holder name, share count, class, and percentage ownership calculated by the platform).

After all entries are made, pull up the resulting cap table summary and verify that: (a) all founders are listed with the correct share counts, (b) the total issued shares match what I specified, and (c) ownership percentages look correct relative to total authorized/issued shares.

Report back with a summary table showing each founder, shares issued, share class, and resulting ownership percentage, plus a note confirming the entries were saved successfully in the platform. Flag any discrepancies or fields the platform required that I didn't originally specify.

You are helping me record investments and SAFEs into our startup's cap table so every informal or formal round is tracked accurately from day one.

- Attach or link the signed instrument to the transaction record if the platform supports document attachment.
- After entering all records, review the resulting cap table summary and flag any entries where a required field was missing from the source document or where the platform requires a value you don't have.
- Do not resolve ambiguous terms yourself — this is a drivable, self-contained data-entry task, but any conflicting or missing terms should be listed for me to clarify.

Report back with: a list of all investments/SAFEs entered, the fields recorded for each, any discrepancies or missing data flagged for my review, and a link or screenshot reference to the updated cap table.

You are helping me prepare for a verification review of our startup's cap table before I formally sign off on it. Please do the following:

1. Ask me where our cap table currently lives (e.g., a spreadsheet file, Carta, Pulley, or another cap table tool) and where our supporting legal documents are stored (e.g., safes, convertible notes, stock purchase agreements, board consents, 83(b) elections).
2. Using your configured credentials, access the cap table and the underlying documents.

4. Flag any discrepancies, missing documents, duplicate entries, or rounds not yet reflected (including informal or handshake investments that lack paperwork).
5. Produce a clear discrepancy report organized by holder, showing what the cap table says versus what the documents say, and list any holders with no supporting document at all.
6. Prepare a summary checklist of everything that needs my review: confirmed-accurate entries, entries needing correction, and entries needing new or missing paperwork.
7. Do not modify the cap table, mark anything as verified, or communicate to investors or stakeholders that the cap table is accurate.

Once you have the discrepancy report and checklist ready, present them to me and stop for human sign-off, since only I as an authorized officer can attest that the cap table matches legal reality. Report back with the discrepancy report, the checklist, and a short summary of the overall state of the cap table (e.g., number of clean entries vs. entries needing attention).

You are helping me export the current, authoritative cap table so we can reconcile it against recent SAFEs, grants, and transfers before board approval. If the platform only allows an on-screen or PDF report, capture that instead and note the limitation.

Save the export with a clear filename indicating the source and as-of date (e.g., 'CapTable_Carta_2025-05-30.xlsx'). Do not modify any values in the platform itself — this is a read-only export step.

When done, report back: which platform you pulled from, the as-of date of the export, the file name/format, total number of holders and securities included, and any discrepancies, missing data, or access issues you encountered (e.g., pending transactions not yet reflected, or fields you couldn't export). Flag anything that looks stale or incomplete so I can address it before reconciliation.

You are helping me reconcile recent cap table transactions before board approval. Please prepare (but do not finalize or approve) a reconciliation package.

- Where signed legal documents live (e.g., a folder in Google Drive, Dropbox, or a signing tool like DocuSign) for recent SAFEs, grants, and transfers
- The date range or list of transactions to reconcile

Then:

4. Flag any mismatches, missing documents, or entries with no corresponding signed document, and flag any signed documents with no corresponding cap table entry.
5. Produce a reconciliation summary table listing: transaction ID, holder, type, cap table values, document values, match status (match/mismatch/missing), and notes on discrepancies.

Done looks like: every recent transaction has been checked against its underlying legal document, a clear discrepancy list exists, and no changes have been made to the cap table itself.

Because judging whether each entry legally matches its document requires human legal/financial judgment, you must not correct entries, approve the reconciliation, or mark it board-ready. Report back with the full comparison table, a short list of flagged discrepancies needing my review, and any documents you couldn't locate — then stop for human sign-off.

You are helping me draft a board consent (unanimous written consent or consent resolution) approving recent cap table changes—e.g., new SAFEs, option grants, or share transfers—for my company. Once the draft is complete, save it as a document (e.g., in Google Docs or as a Word/PDF file) and share the link or file with me for legal and board review. Do not send it to board members or request signatures yourself—circulating for execution remains a human step. Report back with a summary of the transactions included, any flagged gaps needing my confirmation, and the location of the draft file.

You are helping me prepare the board consent that approves recent cap table changes (new SAFEs, option grants, and/or share transfers) before I send it to the board for signature. Cross-check the drafted numbers against the current cap table export to confirm they reconcile — flag any discrepancy before finalizing. Prepare a short cover note summarizing what's being approved, suitable for emailing to directors.

Once the draft and cover note are ready, stop for human sign-off and report back: the draft consent text, the cover note, any reconciliation discrepancies found, and a checklist of what I still need to do (send to directors, collect signatures, file the executed consent). You are helping me prepare for a cap table audit ahead of a fundraise. The goal of this step is to gather and organize all investor-related documents so ownership, board consents, and investor rights can be verified.

Organize these into a single folder structure or index (by round, then by document type) so they can be cross-referenced against the cap table.

As you go, flag any gaps: missing signatures, missing board consents, rounds with no corresponding agreement, or investors listed on the cap table without supporting documents. Produce a checklist noting which documents are present, which are missing, and which need human review for accuracy or legal interpretation.

When done, report back with: a summary of documents found and organized, the folder/index structure created, a list of gaps or missing items flagged for follow-up, and any documents whose validity or completeness you're unsure about. Do not attempt to interpret legal sufficiency or sign anything — this remains a human step for legal review.

You are helping me prepare a cap table accuracy audit ahead of a fundraise. I will provide (ask me if missing): (1) the current cap table file (spreadsheet or export from our cap table management tool), (2) a folder or repository location containing signed source documents — stock certificates, SAFEs, convertible notes, option grants/exercise agreements, board consents authorizing issuances, and any warrant agreements, and (3) my company domain/name for labeling outputs.

Please do the following:

3. Cross-reference each cap table line item against its corresponding source document, flagging: missing documents, quantity mismatches, missing board consent for an issuance, missing signatures, or terms (e.g., liquidation preference, pro-rata rights, vesting schedule) present in the document but not reflected on the cap table.
4. Produce a discrepancy report organized by holder, listing each flagged item, the cap table value, the document value, and the document link/filename for reference.
5. Note any documents you could not locate or open, and any holders on the cap table with no matching document found.

Once the discrepancy report and document cross-reference are complete, stop for human sign-off so I can review materiality and decide on corrections before the raise. Report back with the discrepancy report, a summary count of clean vs. flagged entries, and the list of missing/unmatched documents.

You are helping me prepare a board consent review as part of a cap table audit before a fundraise. I need you to organize and index all board consent/resolution documents so I can personally judge completeness and validity — you will not make legal judgments yourself.

Then: locate every board consent, written resolution, or meeting minute related to equity issuances, option pool increases, officer/director appointments, and investor rights grants. For each equity issuance line in the cap table, attempt to match it to a corresponding board consent document. Build a table with columns: issuance/grant (recipient, security type, date, amount), matching board consent found (yes/no/partial), consent date, and file location/link. Flag any issuances with no matching consent, consents missing signatures or dates, or consents that reference the wrong terms (e.g., mismatched share counts or prices).

Summarize your findings as a checklist: total issuances reviewed, count fully documented, count missing or incomplete, and a list of specific gaps needing my attention (e.g., "Series A investor rights consent — no signature page found").

Do not decide whether any consent is legally sufficient or complete — that judgment is mine. Once your index and gap list are ready, stop for human sign-off and present the checklist so I can review each flagged item before we proceed with the audit.

You are helping me prepare an attorney sign-off package for our cap table audit ahead of a fundraise. This is a policy-gate step: a licensed attorney must personally review and certify compliance, so you must prepare all materials and then stop for human sign-off — do not certify, approve, sign, or submit anything on my behalf, and do not contact the attorney directly unless I've given you their email and asked you to send the draft.

First, ask me for anything missing: (1) location/link to our current cap table file, (2) board consent records, (3) investor rights documents (e.g., ROFR, pro-rata, information rights agreements), (4) any prior legal review notes, (5) the name/firm and contact info of the attorney handling sign-off, and (6) our target raise timeline.

Once you have these, do the following:

2. Flag any gaps or inconsistencies you notice (e.g., missing signatures, undocumented grants, mismatched share counts) in a clearly labeled 'Open Questions for Counsel' section.
3. Draft a short cover email to the attorney summarizing the raise context, attaching/linking the packet, and requesting written sign-off confirming the cap table and instruments comply with applicable securities and corporate law.
4. Save the packet and draft email in a shared location I specify, and give me a checklist of what's included and what still needs my input.

Calculate a draft composite risk score using the rubric weights, and note which approval tier this would fall into (e.g., low/medium/high risk) based on our thresholds if provided.

Compile everything into a single summary document: vendor name, category-by-category scores with justifications, flagged concerns, draft composite score, and suggested risk tier — clearly labeled as a DRAFT for human review.

Do not finalize the risk rating or make an approval decision yourself — a human security reviewer must judge the actual exposure and finalize the score given SOC 2 compliance stakes. Present the completed draft package and then stop for human sign-off, reporting back what you assessed, what you flagged, and what remains for the reviewer to confirm or override.

Report back with: a summary of what was prepared, the location/filenames of the drafts, the checklist of open items, and confirmation that everything is staged and awaiting the officer's signature.

1. Compile a per-state table showing: total revenue, transaction count, and the applicable economic nexus threshold (both the revenue dollar amount and, where relevant, the transaction count) for each state where I have sales.
2. For each state, calculate how close I am to or how far past the threshold I am, noting the specific rule (e.g., revenue-only threshold vs. revenue-or-count threshold, and any look-back period used).
3. Flag states where thresholds appear clearly crossed, states that are borderline/ambiguous (e.g., near the threshold, unclear transaction counting rules, marketplace-facilitator exclusions), and states clearly below threshold.
4. Note any data gaps or inconsistencies (e.g., missing transaction counts, refunds not netted out) that could affect the determination.
5. Prepare a summary document listing your proposed nexus determination per state, with the supporting numbers and your confidence/flag level, ready for my review.

Done looks like: a clear, well-organized per-state summary with data, threshold comparisons, and flags, plus a short list of open questions or ambiguous cases for me to resolve.

Do not register with any state, mark any state as confirmed nexus, or take any action based on the determination — this requires my judgment given the legal and financial exposure. Report the compiled summary and flagged items back to me and then stop for human sign-off.

You are helping me prepare state sales tax registrations after our nexus study identified which states require us to register. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: (a) the list of states where we have established nexus (from our completed nexus study), (b) our legal business name, EIN, business address, entity type, and NAICS code, (c) the name, title, and contact info of the responsible officer who will attest the registrations (do not ask for their SSN), and (d) our expected first taxable sale date in each state.

2. Visit https://www.streamlinedsalestax.org/ and check which of our nexus states participate in the Streamlined Sales Tax (SST) registration system, since that allows a single application to cover multiple member states. Note the SST registration requirements and any documents needed.

3. For each nexus state not covered by SST, navigate to that state's Department of Revenue website, and document: the registration portal URL, required information fields, filing frequency options, any registration fees, and estimated processing time.

4. Using the business details I provide, pre-fill or draft the registration data for each state (business info, NAICS code, expected sales, filing frequency choice) in a clear document or spreadsheet, organized by state, so the responsible officer can review and submit quickly.

5. Compile a checklist per state showing: registration portal link, required fields, documents needed, and a blank spot for the responsible officer's attestation/signature.

Important: Do not submit any registration, attest to any information, or enter the responsible officer's SSN or EIN into any state portal — designating the responsible party and submitting SSN/EIN-linked information creates a binding legal tax obligation, so this remains a human step. Prepare everything needed and then stop for human sign-off.

Report back with the compiled state-by-state checklist, pre-filled data drafts, links to each portal, and a clear list of what I still need to review and personally submit.

You are helping me enable automatic sales tax calculation and collection on checkout and invoices using {{vendor}}, our payments/billing tax platform, now that we've completed our nexus study and state registrations. Use your configured credentials to access {{vendor}} and our billing/checkout system.

Before starting, ask me for: (1) the {{vendor}} account/workspace to use if not obvious, (2) the list of states (or countries, if VAT/GST applies) where we're now registered and should collect tax, (3) the effective date collection should start, and (4) whether both checkout (new transactions) and invoicing (recurring/existing customers) need to be updated, or just one.

Then:
1. In {{vendor}}, locate the automatic tax calculation setting for the account and enable it.
2. Configure the tax settings so calculation is active only for the jurisdictions I confirmed are registered — do not enable collection for states where we have no nexus or registration on file.
3. Verify that the checkout flow and invoice generation are both wired to call {{vendor}}'s tax calculation via its documented API (or dashboard integration) so tax is computed and applied automatically on every new transaction and invoice going forward.
4. Run or trigger a small number of test transactions/invoices (sandbox or test mode if available) across a few of the confirmed states to confirm correct tax rates are calculated and applied at checkout and on invoices.
5. Document any jurisdictions where calculation could not be enabled (e.g., missing registration info) and flag them.

Done means: automatic tax calculation is live for all confirmed registered jurisdictions on both checkout and invoices, and test transactions show correct tax applied.

Report back with: which jurisdictions now have tax collection enabled, test transaction results, any jurisdictions skipped or failed with reasons, and confirmation the integration is calling {{vendor}} automatically for new transactions.

You are helping me finish setting up sales tax compliance automation. My business is already registered for sales tax in one or more states and I have an active {{vendor}} tax-automation account connected to my billing/payment system. Your job now is to configure {{vendor}} so that recurring state sales tax returns are prepared, filed, and remitted automatically, on autopilot, going forward.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available in the {{vendor}} account: the full list of states where I'm registered, my assigned filing frequency per state (monthly/quarterly/annual), the effective start date for each registration, and the email address that should receive filing notifications and confirmations.

Then, using your configured credentials, log into {{vendor}} (dashboard or API) and:
1. Confirm each registered jurisdiction is active in the platform's nexus/registration list.
2. Set up or verify the recurring filing schedule for every jurisdiction, matching each state's required frequency and due dates.
3. Enable automatic remittance so tax collected is paid to each state without manual intervention, and confirm the on-time filing guarantee (penalty coverage) is active for these jurisdictions.
4. Turn on the calendar/dashboard view showing upcoming returns, per-filing status, and amounts remitted, and confirm downloadable confirmation receipts will be generated for each filed return.
5. Set up notification alerts for filing success, failure, or any required action.

Done looks like: every registered state has a recurring filing job scheduled with the correct frequency, automatic remittance enabled, guarantee coverage confirmed, and the filing calendar populated with upcoming due dates.

Report back with: the list of jurisdictions now on autopilot, their filing frequencies and next due dates, confirmation that remittance and the late-filing guarantee are active, and where I can view the ongoing filing calendar and download confirmations.

You are helping me invite a new teammate to our {{vendor}} workspace with the correct access level. Before starting, ask me for any of the following if not already known: the teammate's email address, the {{vendor}} workspace/organization name or URL, the intended access level (e.g., full member, guest/limited access, or admin), and whether they should be added to any specific channels (public or private) upon joining.

Once you have this information, using my configured credentials, log into the {{vendor}} admin or workspace settings area and:

2. Enter the teammate's email address.
3. Set their access level according to my instructions — if they are an external partner or collaborator, use a guest account or limited-access role rather than full membership; if they are a full internal teammate, assign standard member access (or admin, only if explicitly requested).

Done looks like: the teammate has a pending or accepted invite in {{vendor}} with the correct access level (guest/limited or full member) and correct channel memberships as specified.

Report back to me with: the teammate's email, the access level granted, any channels they were added to, and the current invite status (pending/accepted). If the {{vendor}} interface requires any confirmation or approval step that only an account owner can complete, note that this remains a human step and stop there.

You are helping me track the status of a teammate invitation I sent as part of onboarding a new org member. The actual acceptance of the invite email and account setup (name, password, etc.) must be completed by the invited teammate themselves on their own timeline — this remains a human step and you cannot perform it or fill it in on their behalf.

What I need from you: please ask me for (1) the name/email of the invited teammate, (2) the platform or tool they were invited to (e.g., our project management tool, cloud provider, CRM, etc.), and (3) where I can check invite status (admin/team/members dashboard URL or app name) if I haven't already provided it.

5. Note the date/time you checked so I can track how long the invite has been outstanding.

Done looks like: you've confirmed the current status of the invite and reported back clearly whether it's still pending or has been accepted, along with the assigned access level if visible, plus a draft reminder ready if needed. Report back with the status, timestamp checked, and any draft text prepared. Do not attempt to accept the invite or set up credentials on the teammate's behalf — only they can do that.

You are helping me complete a teammate onboarding step in {{vendor}}, our team-chat tool. A new member has already been invited to the organization and had their access level set. Your job now is to add them to the right channels and confirm their access is correct.

Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available in your configured credentials or context, specifically:
1. The new teammate's name or account identifier in {{vendor}}.
2. The list of channels they should join (public and/or private), based on their team or role.
3. Whether they need guest/external-partner-level access to any shared channels, or full internal member access.

Done looks like: the teammate is a confirmed member of every listed channel, with the correct access level (internal or guest) in each, and no channel membership or permission mismatches remain.

Report back to me with: the teammate's name, the final list of channels they were added to, their access level in each, any channels that required special (guest/external) handling, and confirmation that audit logging (if applicable) captured these changes.
